speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this week the 16 Foreign Ministers of the NATO countries meet for the Alliance's thirty-fifth anniversary meeting. "Peace and freedom through deterrence" has been NATO's strategy since 1949, and it has been a successful one. This strategy has worked as a deterrent to Soviet aggression since 1949 because
NATO members have remained firm in their resolve, despite the best efforts of the peace movement, that pledging a no first use of nuclear weapons would encourage Moscow to launch a conventional attack on western Europe.
At the Atlantic Treaty Association conference last year NATO Secretary General, Joseph Luns, made the following observation:
It has always been an imbalance in weaponry and manpower, coupled with a desire to impose one's will on others by force, which has led nations to consider it worth the risk of beginning a war .. . The safest way to preserve peace is to ensure as close a balance as possible between the arsenals on each side.
That is the principle which must guide the Alliance in the future as we seek fair and verifiable agreements with the Soviet Union.
As Canadians we must live up to the goals to which we are committed. Estimates of defence expenditures as a percentage of Gross Domestic Product for 1983 place us at the bottom of all NATO partners with 2.1 per cent, just ahead of Luxembourg. Our NATO partners deserve and expect more from us in the future.

subsubtopic: UNDERLYING PRINCIPLES-PLEA FOR PROCLAMATION OF DAY OF PRAYER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the very First paragraph in the Constitution Act, 1981, which is Canada's Constitution, states: "Whereas Canada is founded upon the principles that recognize the supremacy of God and the rule of law."
Just how would the Supreme Court interpret and uphold these principles? So I dare ask this Parliament, which passed this Constitution Act, what are these principles? Where are they transcribed? How is this nation, Canada, which is founded upon these principles, to know these principles? Are these principles taught in our schools, in our homes, in our churches, or in our institutions?
On November 23, 1983, I suggested in this assembly that this Parliament proclaim a Day of Prayer in Canada in early 1984, a day on which each of us might dwell upon these principles, a day on which we might all pray for world peace and brotherhood, a day on which each of us, after his or her own manner, can quietly recognize the supremacy of God.

The House resumed from Tuesday, May 29, consideration of the motion of Mr. LeBlanc that Bill C-37, an Act to amend the National Housing Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in the debate on Bill C-37, an Act to amend the National Housing Act. I am pleased that the Minister is present here today because I have a number of points to make of which he should be aware regarding matters which are causing some concern to my constituents, to those in the housing industry and to those in the finance industry of the country. I think those issues must be addressed by the Government in the committee.
We know that the Act basically does three things. It provides for mortgage rate insurance, it provides for mortgage-backed securities and it provides for moving the Rural and Native Housing Program into the exclusive domain of the federal Government. As I go through my review of the Bill in the House today, I will deal with those matters one at a time.
I would like to begin by dealing with the Mortgage Rate Protection Plan. In committee we will be asking for the background papers for this Mortgage Rate Protection Plan because we have had no access to the background studies which have been done on those proposals. There are many questions which must be answered. Will the program be a money-maker? How was the amount deductible arrived at? How was the fee to be charged arrived at? What were the figures that were used to design the plan itself and to come to a fee of 1.5 per cent on a maximum mortgage of $70,000 which means a fee of $1,050? How was the deductible of 2 per cent arrived at?
May 30, 1984

I have some thoughts of my own regarding that 2 per cent deductible since I am by nature suspicious of plans that are brought forward by this Government. Perhaps now is a good time to comment on that deductible. I have reviewed the record of five-year mortgages from 1951 to 1984. It is interesting to note that from 1951 to 1955 there was an increase of less than 2 per cent in mortgage interest rates. From 1955 to 1960 there was an increase of less than 2 per cent. There was an increase of less than 2 per cent between 1960 and 1965. From 1965 to 1970 there was an increase of exactly 3 per cent and anyone who had such insurance at that time would not have been helped very much. From 1970 to 1975 the increase was less than 2 per cent. From 1975 to 1979 the increase was less than 2 per cent.
The only period of time such an insurance plan would have taken effect was when the present Government was in power and we saw mortgage interest rates skyrocket from 13 per cent right up to 21.5 per cent between December, 1980 and September, 1981. At that time such a scheme would have made some difference. However, if someone had taken out a mortgage at 17 per cent in December, 1981 and by July, 1982 the rate had gone up to 19 per cent again, the mortgage insurance scheme would not have come into effect during that period of time. Mortgage rates then dropped rather dramatically and went down to 12.5 per cent. They are now up to approximately 14.75 per cent. Again an insurance scheme would not come into play.
I now think I understand where the Government got the deductible figure of 2 per cent. The record over the last 34 years shows that there has never been a large enough increase in mortgage interest rates for an insurance scheme to take effect except for the brief period of time when the Liberals forced mortgage interest rates up to about 21.5 per cent. At that time every Member of the House heard very sad stories from people who had lost their homes because of those exorbitantly high interest rates. The best shot the federal Government can make in trying to alleviate the problem is this mortgage insurance protection plan.
I have some concerns that I would like to discuss. Perhaps I could make some positive suggestions to the Minister who is present in the House. I appreciate the fact that he is present and is listening to this debate. First, the maximum mortgage amount to be insured by the Government is $70,000. This limit causes concern in some areas of the country. It causes particular concern in large metropolitan areas like the area of Brampton. It does not pertain as much to the Georgetown portion of my riding but it does cause some concern for Brampton, the Mississauga area, Toronto, perhaps Vancouver and possibly even Ottawa as well. In those areas the maximum of $70,000 is not high enough. That may be the first problem with which we are faced.
It might be worth while for the Minister to take a look at the situation to see if there could not be regional limits which differentiate between areas much like those for the NHA insurance. That insurance scheme applies differently in different areas of the country. That is something that might be
National Housing Act
looked at because I am not sure that the maximum of $70,000 is realistic in some areas of the country today considering the sizes of mortgages that are being assumed.
Another thing that concerns me about that limit is that it is being included in the legislation. That means that that maximum limit remains in the legislation and if we wanted it changed we would have to return to the House to amend the Act. This Bill mentions regulations in 22 places. Heaven knows, that frightens me enough, yet I am here suggesting another regulation. I may be accused of speaking out of both sides of my mouth, but I would like to indicate to the Minister that it may be worth while to take a look at that maximum being in the regulations in order that it can be adjusted from time to time. As he knows, real estate appreciates. It is the one hedge against inflation which people in this country have. I would ask the Government to take that under advisement.
The next matter I would like to speak about is the protection fee. The protection fee of 1.5 per cent is identical whether you take out a one-year mortgage, a three-year mortgage or a five-year mortgage. There is no variation. The best deal, therefore, for anyone who takes out this insurance is a five-year mortgage. It only makes sense. That will cause terrific problems within the financing community. Let us take, for example, a 1.5 per cent increased rate on a one-year mortgage. If a person renews their mortgage for one year and they buy the insurance plan, for them to break even on the insurance plan, the mortgage rate will have to rise 5 per cent in one year. If that person takes out a three-year mortgage and buys the insurance plan, the mortgage rate will have to rise 4 per cent in the three-year period for that person to break even. However, the mortgage rate would only have to increase 3 per cent over a five-year period for that person to break even.
I fiddled with those figures last night. They are approximate, but generally speaking those are the figures. Therefore, the best deal is to renew a mortgage for five years and buy mortgage insurance. The problem is, if there is not a fee which differs from the rate and the length of time for which a person renews his mortgage, tremendous pressure is placed on GICs. Horrendous pressure is placed on the mortgage companies. The upward pressure on GICs for five-year terms will be severe.
As the Minister knows, financial institutions attempt to balance their mortgage loans with their term investment. If it is a five-year mortgage, the mortgage companies attempt to place that up against a five-year GIC. I am concerned about this and I think it is something which the Government should look into. It might look at a rate which varies for a one-year, three-year and Five-year mortgage, to avoid upward pressure on one of the financial segments; the GICs. If there is upward pressure on five-year GICs, then the rates will increase. There is no question that the rates will go up. If the rates go up, it follows that mortgage rates will go up. I think that is something the Minister and his Department should look into. It concerns me that all of a sudden there will be great interest in

May 30, 1984
National Housing Act
five-year mortgages and, therefore, the upward pressure on GICs will be out of control. The resultant increase would be reflected in mortgage rates. That is another concern. We do not want to see those rates go any higher. Even though there will be a mortgage insurance plan to cover that increase, we do not want to see them go any higher.
Another concern is that if there is a tremendous demand on the five-year GIC, that would crowd out the five-year bond market. There would be an emphasis on where that money would be invested. I hope the Minister will take these concerns into consideration.
I am concerned as well that the Bill places restrictions on the eligibility of mortgages. There are three groups of people the Bill does not cover. The first group is those people who took out mortgages before March 1, 1984. If we look at mortgage rates before March 1, 1984, we see that they were approximately 12.5 per cent. Today those rates have risen to 14.25 per cent or 14.5 per cent. The people who took mortgages out before March 1 are the people who are genuinely interested in the plan because they have already seen the rate rise 2 per cent. Those people are not protected and will not be protected. That is a segment of the population which will not be able to participate in this plan for a considerable length of time.
There is a second group which will not be protected under the plan. If a person purchases a home-it may be his first home-which is not a new home but a resale, and if there is a mortgage on the home which is not insured, that person cannot insure the new mortgage which he will be assuming on the home. Therefore, the purchaser of that home cannot take advantage of the plan if there is an existing mortgage as well, if the vendor does not have insurance coverage, then the purchaser cannot get it by taking over an existing mortgage. As the Minister knows, that happens all the time in the used house market. I think these concerns must be addressed.
There is a third group which would not be covered by this plan. If a person bought a home and the vendor took back the first mortgage, then the purchaser could not buy insurance on the mortgage which the vendor would take back. That person would be excluded. The only way that that person might be able to buy a home is if the vendor wanted to make an investment in the mortgage and took back the first mortgage. However, the purchaser would not be allowed to opt into the insurance plan. Those are three areas which require consideration.
Another area which is covered by the Bill is the mortgage-backed securities. This provision is designed, of course, hopefully to provide longer-term mortgages for home owners. Traditionally, we consider interest rates that are provided over and above any investment for five years are usually 1 per cent to
1.5	per cent higher. If it is a ten-year investment, it would probably be 1 per cent to 1.5 per cent higher. Therefore, if we get into longer-term mortgages, that will increase mortgage rates. I would recommend to a person buying a home that they not get into a ten-year mortgage situation, but that is not my decision. However, those people will be paying a much higher
interest rate than they would pay if they had a five-year mortgage.
I would like to refer to another Bill which is not before the House at the moment, Bill C-36. The prepayment penalty situation would be horrendously expensive for anyone who had less than a ten-year mortgage. They would be paying a much larger penalty than others on a prepayment penalty. That would present a problem. As the Minister knows, a vehicle being used in the United States can be traded on the open market. I understand that a Bill was passed in the House in 1976 or 1977 which was called the Mortgage Exchange Corporation. All that Bill needs is proclamation. That Bill would allow those mortgage-backed securities to be traded on the open market. I do not know the disposition of that Bill right now; however, the Minister might be able to enlighten the House on that situation.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), who is also in the House, promised in his Budget that the federal Government would investigate the economic and financial impact of this legislation on the housing market, mortgage rates and on competing ten-year financial instruments. I ask now if in fact that investigation has taken place, and if so, I would hope that that study is produced so that we could, while we are in committee investigating this particular Bill, be very responsible in our approach to it. We will then have the information which I believe is needed for us to make a balanced decision on this particular proposal which is contained within the Bill.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to see that the federal Government will be taking over the entire responsibility in the area of Indian housing. We are extremely concerned about Indian housing. The testimony which was given to us in the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates within the last month or so indicated that the funding which is available now is barely keeping up with maintaining and bringing up to standard the homes which are already in existence, not to mention new homes for new family formations, and certainly not considering the demand which may come for housing on reserves if other matters are considered in this House.
I am pleased, however, to see that the limit on the total amount to be spent has been increased. I am pleased that the Government has taken that over. Some of my provincial friends may not be too pleased about it, especially in the rural end of the Act as opposed to the Indian people end of the Act, but I am personally pleased that the federal Government has taken that responsibility over completely. I feel in that manner we might be able to make decisions much more quickly. We would be able to establish a housing plan or program without having to depend on the policies and decisions of provincial governments. When it comes to Indian housing, I believe that is going to be very important. Therefore, I congratulate the Minister on that initiative.
I will close my remarks by saying that if this is the best the Government can do, I suppose we will have to put up with it-
May 30, 1984

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: There follows a period of up to ten minutes for questions and/or comments. If there are no questions, we will continue debate.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today in support of Bill C-37, an Act to amend the National Housing Act which introduces a mortgage interest rate protection program and encourages the introduction of longer-term mortgages. These proposals were contained in my February Budget and were included in the Budget in response to two important concerns. First was the need to increase security and certainty for home owners in view of the wide fluctuations in mortgage interest rates which were experienced in the last few years. The second concern was to create conditions which will permit the private sector to develop a longer-term mortgage market in Canada. I must say that in my pre- Budget consultations with the housing industry, which recognizes the importance of developing greater confidence and stability in home ownership, I found that these concerns were very widely shared indeed.
The Bill before the House is the result of extensive postBudget consultations with mortgage lenders, housing associations, the Consumer's Association of Canada and other interested parties. In these sessions the implications of the program and the various administrative and technical issues associated with the program were thoroughly discussed. This consultative process has led to a Bill which should receive wide support from the public, and I was happy to hear the general reaction of the previous speaker in that regard.
While some concern had been expressed that consultations would lead to a delay in implementing the Bill in good time, it appears that we have been able to meet that timetable quite effectively. I would hope that all Parties will support the legislation so that Canadian home owners will be able to obtain this protection without further delay.

Both the Mortgage Rate Protection Program and mortgage-backed Securities will make home ownership easier and safer, by taking away much of the uncertainty caused by fluctuating interest rates.

As Hon. Members know, these initiatives are linked to amendments to the Interest Act which have also been introduced in the House. This legislation will strengthen borrowers' rights and increase the flexibility of the mortgage market. In
National Housing Act
effect, we believe it will allow the reintroduction into the market of mortgages for a longer period than five years, which have practically disappeared from the market for a long time. The value of the housing initiatives in the Budget and particularly the mortgage interest rate protection program has been widely recognized. The head of the Canadian Institute of Public Real Estate Companies has said that the mortgage plan, and I quote:
-will lead the way in other countries in developing stability in the mortgage market.
Mr. Logan Tait of the Canadian Real Estate Association said that the mortgage interest rate plan, and I quote:
-will definitely help to bring stability back into the marketplace.
Mr. John Sandusky, President of HUDAC, now the Canadian Home Builders' Association, said that the Government had, and I quote:
-responded very favourably to our concerns.
On May 29, Mr. Sandusky sent a telegram to a number of Members of the House, including myself, which reads as follows:
The 5,000 member-firms of the Canadian Homebuilders' Association formerly HUDAC urge quick passage to second reading of housing legislation re: Mortgage Rate Plan, Mortgage-backed Securities, and Interest Act amendments.
It is signed John Sandusky, President of Canadian Homebuilders Association.

Mr. Speaker, housing has always been one of the Canadian Government's main priorities, and over the last three years, the Government has introduced a number of measures designed to help homeowners.
The Canada Mortgage Renewal Program was set up towards the end of 1981, and upgraded the following year, to help home owners in financial difficulty when they had to renew their mortgages. Homeowners faced with increases in mortgage costs representing more than 30 per cent of their income became eligible for non-taxable grants of up to $3,000. More than 20,000 Canadians in financial difficulty were helped by this plan.
In 1982, the Canadian Home-ownership Stimulation Plan was established, providing $3,000 grants to buyers of newly-built homes. This program has helped more than 260,000 Canadians buying a home for the first time.
In 1983, this Government made it possible for Canadians who bought new homes between April 19, 1983 and March 1, 1985, which is next year, to claim a special tax deduction of up to $10,000, to be contributed to a Registered Home ownership Savings Plan. I may remind the House that this program is still in effect and that Canadians may now make use of the program if they intend to purchase a newly-built home. The program has considerable tax advantages, and I would urge Canadians who have not already done so to find out about the program and see whether they should not consider purchasing

May 30, 1984
National Housing Act
a new home before the program expires on March 1, 1985. I may also remind the House that this Government has made grants available to home owners for the purpose of home renovation. This is another dimension of the housing sector we have had a tendency to neglect in the past and which fortunately has been given increasing attention in the programs of the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. In 1983 alone, more than 47,000 housing units were renovated with CMHC grants, representing a total of $179 million.
Finally, the federal Government has consulted with the major lending institutions and urged them to respond favourably to the requirements of Canadian individuals who take out mortgages and are faced with problems caused by volatile interest rates.
In this legislation the Government is providing a more fundamental and durable response to the problem of uncertainty in mortgage interest rates. The Mortgage Rate Protection Plan, which has been outlined by my colleague, the Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, has received an enthusiastic response from housing market participants. I believe it will give Canadians who choose to participate a reasonable assurance that large, unexpected increases in interest rates will not lead to serious financial difficulties. This is particularly important for firsttime home buyers. Because of the relatively short terms of mortgages available, these buyers must consider whether they can afford the monthly carrying costs on their homes in the future if interest rates increase sharply when they have to renew their mortgages.
Existing home owners will, of course, also benefit. Mortgage rate uncertainty forces many of them to re-evaluate their saving and spending decisions against the possibility that interest rates would be higher on their renewal dates. The Mortgage Rate Protection Plan will offer both of these groups more security in planning for the future. This increased security for home owners will have a positive influence on the home building industry, on the economy and on the well-being of Canadian society generally.
Members should be aware that the program is not intended to protect home owners against all fluctuations in mortgage rates. Instead, for those individuals who choose to participate, it should be viewed as a safety net that will offer security against severe financial disruption. The Government is prepared to share the risks and the costs with the home owner. Thus the protection will cover three-quarters of any cost increase on a mortgage renewal resulting from an increase in mortgage interest rates greater than 2 per cent, to a maximum of ten percentage points. The fee for the Mortgage Rate Protection Plan has been set at the lowest possible level, 1.5 per cent of the mortgage amount to be protected. For a mortgage of $70,000, for instance, this amounts to a maximum premium of $1,050. The benefits provided upon payment of this fee have been extended as far as is consistent with
ensuring the plan remains fiscally responsible. Every effort has been made to enable home owners who want to use the program to do so by offering them the options of paying the fee up front or adding it to the principal amount and amortizing it over the term of the mortgage. This is how, for instance, it has been indicated that you can buy your protection for as low as something between $11 and $12 a month on a $70,000 mortgage. The latter method will allow a person, therefore, to obtain protection for a very small monthly charge.
Entry into the program is voluntary. No one is forced to join the program. Some have argued that the cost is too high for the benefits available. Maybe some will share that view, but home owners who are concerned about the possible impact of rising mortgage rates-and we have seen this happen already since the last Budget-can decide whether this plan meets their own circumstances. Judging by the response to the Budget proposals, there appears to be substantial interest on the part of the public in general in the program. In fact, more than 14,500 Canadians have written to my Department to ask for more information about the housing proposals contained in the February Budget.

Mr. Speaker, as announced in the Budget, one effect of the Bill will be retroactive to March 1, 1984. For instance, someone who took out a 5-year mortgage at 12.5 per cent on March 1 can purchase coverage against mortgage increases, and that coverage will be based on the rate mentioned, provided that applications under the program, plus the fee, are sent to CMHC within 45 days after the Bill is passed. Since mortgage rates have increased from 2 to 2.25 per cent since March 1, the retroactive effect of the Bill may benefit home owners having renewed or taken out a mortgage since that date.
As for the cost of the program, it is difficult to estimate since it will obviously depend on the number of Canadians taking part in the program and what mortgage rates will be in several years. Nevertheless, we can reasonably assume that the net cost of the program will be close to zero, in other words, the program should be self-financing.

Some Members may well ask: Does this mean that the Government is projecting higher mortgage interest rates? As I have stated many times, the Government is doing everything it can to keep interest rates as low as possible. However, we must recognize that we are participants in an international economy and there are many factors beyond our control that can influence Canadian interest rates. Home owners have expressed concern about the potential effect of higher rates. The Government has responded by providing them with a safety net. At the same time we will continue to focus on maintaining interest rates at the lowest level possible. Home owners would certainly not be unhappy, nor would I, if interest rates were to decline and no benefits were ever paid on this program.
May 30, 1984

Now let me turn for a minute to the provision in this Bill regarding mortgage-backed securities. While this has not received the public attention that the Mortgage Rate Protection Program has, it is an important initiative if we wish to see the reintroduction of longer-term mortgages in Canada, those with terms longer than five years. Further, it would provide for a more smoothly functioning mortgage market by providing an alternative method of financing mortgages.

This part of the Bill has also received the firm support of a number of groups, and I am thinking especially of the Canadian Homebuilders' Association, which favours the development of a market for mortgage-backed securities in Canada, which would make it possible to provide more home buyers with mortgages at reasonable cost. The housing sector has stated that 10-year mortgages would be an essential factor in providing for stability and growth in the residential construction industry. In the course of our post-budget consultations with financial market experts, it was clearly stated, as an essential condition for offering mortgage-backed securities in Canada, that conditions for payment of principal and interest on these securities would have to be strictly observed by the private sector.

Members of the House should be aware that the guarantee involves no government subsidy and will operate on a cost-recovery basis. The Government is taking the initiative in establishing a framework which will permit the private sector to develop a market for mortgage-backed securities. Preliminary indications are that there are several institutions interested in pursuing the development of this market if legislation constraints are dealt with. In addition to the timely payment guarantee, the introduction of mortgage-backed securities requires a legislative amendment to the Interest Act with respect to prepayment privileges. The Interest Act amendment is being handled in a separate Bill.

Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind the House that these amendments are supported by the housing industry, home owners and mortgage lenders. I have also received encouragement from Hon. Members on both sides of the House.
For example, following the February Budget the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) said that the housing measures were "nice things that no one is going to be against". On February 21 the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) said: "For our part we welcome mortgage insurance". At the risk of seeming immodest, I will also quote the Hon. Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) who said on February 22: "I, too, commend the courageous Minister of Finance on those parts of the Budget
National Housing Act
that will help housing, such as protecting interest rates and allowing a mortgagor to pay off a mortgage without having to pay an arm and a leg".

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: He said that with tongue in cheek, too.

Members opposite have been eager to deal with this Bill. On May 10 the Hon. Member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. St. Germain) asked why the Mortgage Rate Protection Plan was taking so long. On April 30 the Hon. Member for Simcoe South (Mr. Stewart) said to me: "Before it is too late, Mr. Minister, I ask you on behalf of Canadian home owners and prospective home owners: Where is the beef?"
In view of all that, I would suggest that the Opposition should not hog the Bill in the corner of the House for too long.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: We did not get beef, we got baloney.

I expect Members opposite to act with the sense of importance and urgency which these measures demand. We have heard their expressions of concern over the impact of interest rates on home owners. We share those concerns. This Bill will provide the means for Canadians to protect themselves against the risk of higher mortgage rates. The amendments in this Bill are made in response to the concerns of Canadians about the uncertainty of future mortgage costs. In these proposals we have tried to ensure that the efficient functioning of the mortgage market is not impaired.
Under normal circumstances none of the proposals will impose significant costs on the federal Government although the Government is prepared to provide assistance in extra-ordinary circumstances. I urge all Parties to support these proposals so that Canadian home owners and prospective home buyers will have improved security against the risk of losing their homes because of fluctuations in mortgage rates over which they have no control.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Ten-minute period for questions or comments. Questions? The Hon. Member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle).

Mr. Speaker, my question is of course directed to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). Since mortgage rates today are at about 14.5 per cent, and the Bill provides for an additional 2 per cent, borrowers will be facing rates of 16 or
16.5	per cent, if I understand the program correctly. Is the Minister claiming, with his concept of making home ownership available to all Canadians, that rate of 16.5 per cent is going to encourage people to buy houses? I am not referring to millionaires, I am talking about the average person, the average worker. Does he think this rate is low enough to make home ownership generally accessible?

Mr. Speaker, of course, my answer would depend on the financial climate at the time. I may remind the Hon. Member that even when mortgage rates were at 18 per

May 30, 1984
National Housing Act
cent, 19 per cent or 20 per cent, people were still buying homes. In any case, we must consider the state of the economy at a given time. If we were going through an inflationary period, with inflation at 12 or 13 per cent, as we have experienced in the past, it would not be surprising to see mortgages as high as 16 per cent, while interest on loans would also be very high.
I cannot predict what interest rates will be in five years, for instance when someone's mortgage expires. What the Bill provides is protection against interest rates that may prevail at the time people have to renew their mortgages. It is a little like fire insurance. When a person takes out fire insurance, he does not particularly want to collect. His reasoning is that if something happens, at least he will be covered. When people take out fire insurance, they do not say to themselves: I wish my house would burn down and I could collect the insurance! Unless, of course, they do so for reasons that are neither very legal or ethical. Insurance is a kind of protection, and that is what we are offering today, protection against events that would not be to the advantage of the borrower. I think the best analogy is still fire insurance or accident insurance. Nobody wants to have an accident, nobody wants his house to burn down, but everyone buys insurance, thinking: "If it happens, at least I am covered!" And coverage is what we are providing. If, for instance, interest rates increase by more than 2 per cent in five years, when my mortgage expires I will have the assurance that the Government will pay three-quarters of the difference between 2 per cent and 10 per cent more, for instance, so I am covered.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle), with a supplementary.

The Minister's answer is quite clear and it just means that people who have enough money, and I think that is always the minority ... I would like to ask the Minister whether, for instance, with a family income of $35,000 or less, interest rates at 16 per cent would really make homeownership generally accessible? I have the impression that it would still be very hard for thousands of Canadians who would like to buy a home, even at present rates. I agree that anyone with an income of $40,000 and $50,000 or more can cope with today's rates. But what about young couples and so many other Canadians who earn between $20,000 and $35,000, for instance? Does the Minister of Finance still think that present rates are reasonable for this group of individuals which probably includes most first-home buyers?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is talking about an interest rate of 16 per cent. No one is borrowing at 16 per cent today. The Hon. Member was talking about rates of about 14 or 14.5 per cent for a 5-year period, and he knows as well as I do that lower rates are available for three years or one year. I may also remind the Hon. Member that there are programs to help people on very low incomes. I am thinking of
Co-operative Housing Assistance and similar programs that have been in effect for a number of years, to help people on low incomes who need housing assistance. We do not claim that the Bill before the House today is the answer to all financial problems that may face Canadians who want to buy a home. There will be people on low incomes who will still have to resort to other Government programs designed for their particular needs. What we are offering today is an insurance plan available to all Canadians and which all Canadian home buyers should be able to afford, for a relatively modest fee.
As I said earlier, for a $75,000 mortgage, coverage will cost $11 or $12 per month. This is not excessive in relation to the mortgage amount itself. For a home that costs half as much and with a much lower mortgage, the cost of coverage will be half the amount I just mentioned. With a $35,000 mortgage, the monthly cost will be $5 or $6. I think the advantages are considerable. Here again, no one is forcing Canadians to take advantage of this opportunity, any more than anyone is forcing them to take out fire insurance. I think Canadians should be encouraged to take out this insurance policy, just like the usual insurance policy when they take out a mortgage.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Any other questions or comments?

Mr. Speaker, my question for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) is three-fold. He mentioned repeatedly that he had been consulting with a number of groups, including home owners. Could he share with us in what way he was communicating with home owners to receive input for Bill C-37?
Second, he referred to this insurance plan as being similar to taking out hail or fire insurance. Floods, hail, fire and the like are really acts of God totally unrelated to the works of man. Yet interest rates in other countries, when it comes to mortgages, are set or there is a very definite ceiling allowed. I think specifically of the country of Norway when I make that comment. In a sense we are dealing with man's actions when we talk about interest rates, not acts of God.
Third, the Minister of Finance has indicated his concern many times in the House regarding people who are locked into mortgage rates over a five-year period when interest rates drop substantially. I think he has indicated his interest in a three-year penalty as being a reasonable one under those conditions to allow people to renegotiate their mortgages to take advantage of lower rates. Does the mortgage-backed security aspect take into account this option of a three-month penalty clause being sufficient?

Mr. Speaker, on the first point the Hon. Member knows that we have programs in Canada whereby we put an effective ceiling on the mortgage rates being paid by certain Canadians who are in need. He knows there are
May 30, 1984

programs, for instance, where a person pays 2 per cent for 35 years on his mortgage and CMHC is going to cover the difference. That program is centred on people with lower incomes who need help and support in order to have access to housing.
That is not the type of measure my hon. friend would recommend we apply wholesale. The cost would be horrendous. It would also introduce severe distortions into the economy. We have as much as possible a free market in the mortgage area and in the area of interest rates. The hon. Member knows that we are very dependent upon what is happening in the international community. He talks about acts of God, such as fire and so on. He knows also in the area of interest rates that there are a number of factors over which we have no control domestically. We live in a world with considerable pressures taking place. Canada as a medium-size country is one, suffering particularly from some of the decisions being taken in the United States, which has the largest and strongest economy in the world. It has advantages in some regards, but it also has drawbacks, as the Hon. Member knows.
As far as the other point is concerned, the Hon. Member knows that under the proposed amendments to the Interest Act we have removed the provision concerning the three months' penalty. This has been done following extensive consultations. The Hon. Member asks with whom. I can say that we have had extensive consultations with the Consumers' Association of Canada which comprises hundreds of thousands of Canadians who also happen to be home owners. As I mentioned, 14,500 Canadians have written to me asking for more information on housing. We have consulted with the industry, house builders, et cetera, and found that these people are very interested in selling houses and they have the interest of the potential home buyer very much at heart. They are not interested in building homes just to let them sit empty. Everybody who has an interest in the housing area has been invited to contribute. People have made their contribution, supported the measures we have put forward and the conclusions we have reached.
I hope we will have a very short discussion of this Bill so that it can be considered in committee. We will be very happy to discuss with Hon. Members the details of the measure in committee. I hope in the interests of all Canadians that we can get the Bill considered as quickly as possible.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The period set aside for questions and comments has expired. Debate. The Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis).

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to make some comments regarding Bill C-37, an Act to amend the National Housing Act, which is intended to give some relief to the volatile interest rates affecting mortgage holders. I am pleased to see the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) is in the House as well as the Minister responsible for the Bill.
National Housing Act
I have listened carefully to the observations of a number of Hon. Members regarding Bill C-37. It is important that we recognize the situation in which this Bill is brought forward. We have a very serious housing situation in Canada. Mortgage rates today are in the 14 per cent to 14.5 per cent range which makes home ownership an impossibility now for most Canadians who presently do not own their own homes. Considering that every indicator of which I am aware would suggest there is a good possibility of interest rates increasing in the weeks and months ahead, this gives Canadians cause to believe that the mortgage rates they are paying on their homes will likely increase.
We are talking about a situation of people desiring to be new home owners who are finding it an impossibility today to think seriously about investing in a home. Those who are renegotiating mortgages today and in the weeks and months ahead have serious concerns about the implications of the present high interest rates and the spectre of increasing interest rates. The construction industry has indicated concern as well.
The construction industry in parts of Canada has virtually died. I am thinking particularly of parts of British Columbia and Alberta which for all intents and purposes have no viable housing construction industry at all as a result of the general economic conditions, mortgage interest rates and the uncertainty surrounding the interest rate phenomenon. We are talking about the tens of thousands of manufacturers both large and small which serve the housing construction industry. We find that they too are in a slump situation because new homes are not being built as required.
In the City of Kamloops the mayor wanted to put together a promotional video cassette not too long ago. He asked people in his building department to take pictures of some of the construction going on in the community, but there was no construction going on anywhere in the city. He could not find a person banging on a wall or shingling a roof. People had to manufacture a show of building. That is the situation in a city of 60,000 to 70,000 people.
If you walk around the subdivisions and through the inner cities of Canada, "For Sale" signs have become a reality on most streets. These signs of people moving out of their homes do not reflect a mobility taking place; they reflect growing numbers of Canadians being forced out of their homes or abandoning them.
What has happened is that three or four years ago both husband and wife were working. They could quite easily afford a mortgage payment of $400 or $500, perhaps even a bit higher. They assumed they would have to work, scrimp and save, but making a mortgage payment of $400, $500, or $600 was something they could manage and they entered into a mortgage. Perhaps they tied themselves in for five years or less, but they were into their first home and were part of the home ownership that Canadians have taken to so strongly.
Then one of them was laid off. It might even happen that both were laid off. Interest rates meanwhile have increased. Rather than paying $400, $500, or $600 a month on their

May 30, 1984
National Housing Act
mortgage, they are now required to pay $700, $800, or $900. They are, of course, unable to do so. It takes two, three, or four months of non-payment or partial payment before the axe comes down. For many people the answer is simply to walk away from their home or be forced out by the banks or other financial institutions when they are unable to make their payments. This is an incredible situation, Mr. Speaker.
Members of Parliament, particularly those from western Canada, fly across the country on a weekly basis. They see forests covering the nation from one end to the other. We have thousands and thousands of hectares of forest land. There is space everywhere around our cities. We know the wealth of the country is in place. We know savings accounts and so on, as we are told on a weekly basis, are filled. To have the housing crisis that we have today, you really have to work at it. We have a government that has worked at it and developed it so well that we have literally thousands of Canadians who ought to be living in a home and making mortgage payments today but are not. The housing construction industry is on its knees. It is an incredible situation. Then along comes the Government saying that it has the answer with Bill C-37, the Mortgage Rate Protection Plan.
Let me say at the outset that I will not support this particular program as it has been presented. It is an absolute sham. It is a shame that the Government brings forward a piece of legislation which does not ask the banks to pay any more for the high interest situation. In fact, domestic bank profits are the highest they have ever been in the banking history of the country. That will not be changed one iota. It allows the banks virtually to charge whatever they wish for mortgages.
In effect, the Government of Canada has caused these high interest rates by agreeing to a high interest rate policy, but it will not pay anything in return. Who will pay now to protect themselves from high interest rates? It will not be the Government which created those high rates nor the institutions which benefit from them; it will be Canadian home owners. In other words, they can take out an insurance policy.
As the Minister of Finance said, Canadians are accustomed to taking out insurance policies. They take out hail insurance if they are farmers. They take out fire insurance, theft insurance or whatever. If they take out flood insurance, hurricane insurance, revolution insurance or insurrection insurance on foreign investments, they are dealing with matters completely beyond their control. In many cases they are acts of God. However, what we are dealing with today is the concept of mortgage rates, and that is not an act of God. Perhaps the Minister of Finance would argue against that, since it is his policy, but the point is that interest rates are government policy.
I should like to indicate that this need not be the case. The other day I talked with representatives of the Government of Norway. I asked them what they did about their mortgage rates and how they organized the market in their country. They said that it was simple, that their people could obtain
mortgages at 10 per cent today and the most they will ever have to pay is 12 per cent over a 30-year term. It does not matter if inflation reaches 200 per cent or 300 per cent. It does not matter what happens in terms of the money markets. They have mortgage money for that length of time at a maximum of 12 per cent because the Government of Norway decided that it was important for its people to be able to afford to own their own homes, that it was in the nation's interest.
When the Minister of Finance says that the Government wants Canadians to take out insurance against high interest rates, it is a sham. I think the Government has stepped back from taking responsibility for dealing with high interest rates. As a previous Hon. Member indicated today, this mortgage insurance program does not provide any protection for up to a 2 per cent increase from the day a mortgage is taken out. Today the mortgage rate is 14.5 per cent. What they are saying is that they will allow the rates to go up to at least 16.5 per cent before Canadians obtain any relief whatsoever.
What does it mean when Government Members are asking Canadians to pay at least 16.5 per cent on their mortgages before any relief is provided? Will that bring comfort to the average household in the country? Will people say that they can now afford mortgages at 16 per cent to 16.5 per cent? Some people would say that that is usury, that a 16.5 per cent mortgage rate is totally unacceptable in a country as rich as Canada.
The Government has made an admission that not only is it helpless in this situation, in its own mind, but it is unprepared to deal with the issue as it should. Once again it is asking hard-pressed home owners to carry the can. The Government is asking Canadians to pay premiums which will be 1.5 per cent of their mortgage value. This is to be paid at the time the mortgages are taken out or amortized over the term of the mortgage. On a $70,000 mortgage, that would amount to $1,050 or $11 per month. The insurance will be 2 per cent deductible. In other words, interest rates will have to increase at least 2 per cent before anything is done. If a mortgage were to rise by 6 per cent between the time the mortgage was taken out and its date of renewal, the insurance would not cover the increase resulting from the first 2 per cent. The insurance would cover only three-quarters of the increase in monthly payments over 2 per cent. Therefore, if the rate went up by 6 per cent, which is certainly a possibility in these times, the coverage would be for only 3 per cent of the increase or 50 per cent of the cost.
This is a very expensive piece of insurance. The Government is asking people who are thinking of buying homes to come up with another $1,000 in cash or to be prepared to pay another $11 per month over the term of their mortgage. Quite frankly, we feel this is very misleading.
The Minister of Finance indicated that he has had 14,000 inquiries from Canadians about what the Government was doing to assist them with their mortgages. This does not mean that he has had 14,000 inquiries about Bill C-37. When Canadian citizens find out what really is in Bill C-37, what this mortgage insurance program really means, they will laugh
May 30, 1984

at the Government and say that it cannot be serious if this is its idea of providing Canadians with high interest rate relief. The Government is not prepared to pay a penny itself. It asks Canadian home owners to carry the total burden. Today the Minister of Finance indicated that the Government's intention was not to provide a cent, that it was a break-even plan and that it was a regular insurance program for which people obtaining insurance will pay. Considering that the Government created the situation in part, we feel it is turning its back on its responsibility for encouraging home ownership and assisting Canadians to pay their mortgages.
In a sense it almost rationalizes further interest rates. Then the Government will be able to say that it cannot do anything about high interest rates and that home owners should not be concerned because they can take out insurance if they so wish. I do not think that is a reasonable approach to this matter. We in the New Democratic Party are concerned about the fact that there are other options to pursue. For example, the Government should have the courage and political will to deal with high interest rates. After all, high interest rates in Canada are the problem. We have heard Liberal leadership candidates-and I do not have to name them because the media has done that well-saying that something has to be done about high interest rates. As a matter of fact, one even said that Governor Bouey of the Bank of Canada should be fired because of the advice he has given the Minister of Finance and the Government of Canada.
That was a joke, remember?

It certainly is a joke. The whole approach is a joke. Leading Cabinet Ministers, one after another, agree that action should be taken on high interest rates. We have seen what other countries do when it comes to dealing with interest rates. If we are to provide affordable mortgages for Canadians, we could categorize the group of Canadians we would like to assist, such as Canadians with family incomes below a certain amount. They should be able to obtain funding for mortgages at a set rate from financial institutions. In other words, we should say to the banks of Canada that they have to set aside a certain portion of their loan portfolios to assist home owners and set mortgage rates at 8 per cent or 10 per cent over a prolonged period of time. That is a requirement of the Bank Act. We could ask other financial institutions to follow suit, to make it a fair system. Other countries do that. They have done it for years and years because they realize that home ownership is important and that affordable housing is important. Whether it is rental or home ownership, it is important that people have affordable housing. They take steps to enable their citizens to obtain it. We are not talking about pie in the sky ideas or magical solutions. We simply say to the Government that it should introduce policies that other countries have proven work very effectively. We want the Government to deal with interest rates or, if not, to bring in a special provision.
National Housing Act
Not long ago there was a special provision for small businesses and farmers. It was called the Small Business Development Bond through which money could be borrowed at half prime plus 1 per cent. It cost some money to enable the small business sector to avail itself of money at half prime plus 1 per cent. If it can be done for that particular sector, surely it can be done for others.
Imagine what this could do for the economy of the country. While it may cost the Government a few hundred million dollars in lost revenue, think of what the federal coffers could gain from the increased housing construction that would go on across the country in every community. We would see construction in rural areas as well if people could afford new homes or add to existing homes. It would result in cash circulating within our country and increased sales tax, personal taxes and corporate taxes. It would assist the construction and manufacturing industries. Most importantly, it would allow Canadians to obtain affordable housing of one kind or another.
We look forward to Bill C-37 going to committee. Since we are only discussing the principle of the Bill at this stage, we will be attempting to Fine tune the Bill and to suggest a number of alternatives.
Let me comment on the mortgage-backed securities portion of this Bill. I commend the Government for taking some steps to increase the availability of mortgages beyond five years, but this means that Canadians will once again be locked into interest rates at perhaps 14 per cent to 15 per cent. If interest rates drop they will be told that they can get out of that agreement, but they will have to pay the entire cost of interest to which they agreed. I distinctly remember numerous occasions in the House when the Minister responsible for CMHC and the Minister of Finance said that a 3 per cent penalty clause ought to be adequate. As a matter of fact, the Minister of Finance was surprised that financial institutions were charging more than 3 per cent. We now have legislation that does away with that 3 per cent option once again. We will debate that loudly and push strongly for that option when this Bill gets to committee.
In conclusion, this Bill is not an answer to the high mortgage costs that Canadians are facing today. It is worse than a sham because it gives Canadians the impression that the Government is taking action when all it is doing is telling them that if Canadians want very second-rate insurance coverage to protect them from higher interest rates, this is the vehicle. That is not what the people of Canada deserve and not what the people of Canada should be getting from the Government.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: There follows a ten-minute period for questions and comments.

Mr. Speaker, I am not certain that I will have an opportunity to speak at this stage of the debate so I want to ask the Hon. Member to comment on what I feel is a flaw in this legislation. That is, the effect it will have, if passed, on the
4208

May 30, 1984
National Housing Act
public's lack of will to deal with the fundamental problem of high interest rates which the Hon. Member commented on. If this Bill is passed and people believe that there will be some semblance of protection against increasing interest rates, their will to put pressure on the Government to control those interest rates will wane somewhat. Has the Hon. Member considered how this may reduce some of the political pressure on the Government to take action against the banks that are charging exorbitant rates and reduce some of the pressure on the banking policies of the Liberal Government?

Mr. Speaker, I would be pleased to make a comment in that respect. This Bill gives Canadians the impression that the Government is taking action against high interest rates when it actually shows that the Government is not taking any action at all. The Government is assuming that high interest rates are here to stay and that they are likely to increase. If the Government did not believe that interest rates would increase, there would be no need for this particular Bill. All this Bill does is protect one against increasing interest rates. It does not protect one from being locked into these higher interest rates and enable Canadians to take advantage of lower rates. In fact, it penalizes people because they will not be allowed to take advantage of lower interest rates.
The Government has failed to deal with high interest rates and has based its policies on the assumption that Canadians must follow U.S. interest rates. The Minister of Finance has said that he cannot do anything and must look to Paul Volcker, the Chairman of the Reserve Board in the United States, for guidance. This means that the Government of Canada is saying that a foreign bureaucrat in Washington, D.C. is deciding our monetary policy, the state of the Canadian economy and whether we will stagnate longer, grow, or make matters worse. The Government has no control over what is happening.
I do not believe there is another country in the world whose Minister of Finance would give a foreign bureaucrat all the responsibility to determine its future. The Minister of Finance has made this incredible statement time and again.
In summary, this Bill means that the Government has admitted that interest rates will likely increase and that it plans to do nothing about it. However, if Canadians want to take out very expensive insurance that does not even cover all of their losses as a result of increased rates but simply a portion thereof, they will have the opportunity to do so. I believe it is absurd for the Government to take no action but to introduce the simplistic insurance policy contained in Bill C-37, when we are the richest country in the world with unbelievable resources and a very small population. It does so at a time when there are literally tens of billions of dollars in Canadian savings accounts and a variety of vehicles that would enable the Government to take advantage of lower interest rates. Canadians are interested in getting on with building the economy, of which housing is one option to pursue.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Kam-loops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) commented at some length on the
problems with this Bill. In doing so he pointed out certain shortfalls in other government housing programs that have been undertaken in past years. One of those programs, about which many of my constituents have expressed concern, especially those in the co-operative housing movement, is mentioned in the report of the national task force on co-operative development which was filed with the Government yesterday through the Minister responsible for the Wheat Board. The Minister of State for Economic and Regional Development (Mr. Johnston) suggested in an answer yesterday that he was agreeable with the new co-operative thrust.
Would the Hon. Member elaborate on the impact of the cutbacks in funding from CMHC to the co-operative housing sector? These cuts are in fact destroying the existing structure and support for co-op housing just when the Government seems to be prepared to support more co-op housing and is taking action to protect Canadians against the threat of increased interest rates. Can the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) give us some examples in his area or other areas of British Columbia that are showing the effect of these cutbacks to CMHC funding for housing co-ops on the housing supply in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, I certainly can respond to that question. In my own constituency, we have had the opportunity of developing two co-operative housing complexes. The first one that was built was, I would say, one of the nicest housing developments in the City of Kamloops. There is another co-operative housing complex presently under construction.
I must say that the interest in co-operative housing has risen beyond anyone's wildest dreams, at least in central British Columbia, and I suspect in other areas of the country with which I am familiar as well. Co-operative housing does allow people who would not otherwise be able to afford their own home the opportunity to do so. They have been built extremely well and are being run extremely efficiently. As I say, they allow people to own their own homes.
Unfortunately, while people have been encouraged to start thinking more and more along the lines of co-operative housing, we are being told by CMHC that funding is no longer available. We are being told that while the interest in co-operative housing is appreciated, the fact is that adequate funding is simply not in place. Many people see co-operative housing as a viable housing option, have supported the concept and see its benefits, but they have found that the financing is simply not there. Considering how well it has worked, in spite of the reports of some of the housing construction organizations, it is a shame that we cannot see more support for this kind of housing option. It has been successful in the past and with proper support, it could certainly be successful in the future as well.

Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) whether or not, being the confirmed socialist that I assume he is, he thinks that a housing project which by obligation must make available only 15 per cent of its housing to people of low income is adequate. Mr. Speaker, a short response would be that I agree with the general thrust of the question.
