Mr. Speaker, Bill C-37, an Act to amend the National Housing Act, best typifies the new era of legislation that we have come to expect from the Liberal Government. It follows a pattern that is unfortunately becoming all too common.
Before I make some of the remarks I wish to make on second reading of this Bill regarding its general principle, I would like to acknowledge that since there are about 5.3 million households in Canada, half of which are owned by people who have mortgages on their residences, the intended thrust of this legislation smacks of relief. I say that because we have been told what the legislation will in fact do.
We have all seen the little booklets that were published immediately following the release of the Budget by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) on February 15 of this year, and we all recognize that since that date, interest rates in Canada have risen by between 2 per cent and 2.5 per cent depending upon the term of the mortgage. The larger increase applies to mortgages with one-year terms and the lower increase, although the higher rate, applies to mortgages with terms of five years. We are now looking at interest rates of roughly 12.75 per cent on mortgages with one-year terms and 14.5 per cent on mortgages with five-year terms, with the expectation that those rates will increase. Accordingly, if this Bill were ever to be of any value, it would be of value now because of the built-in advantage to mortgagors who will take advantage of the Bill since it dates back to March 1. From February 15 to March 1, interest rates did not change appreciably.
National Housing Act
Let me briefly explain to the House what I understand to be the general terms of the Bill. The provisions of the Bill are such that it appears that for a fee of 1.5 per cent of the face value of the secured obligation up to a maximum of $70,000, the mortgagor will be entitled to have that portion of payment under a protected mortgage paid to the extent of 75 per cent thereof by the corporation after self-insuring to the extent of 2 percentage points. I say that it appears to do so because I am not too sure that the legal language used accomplishes the alleged purpose. I believe that mortgagors should understand that that is indeed the case. The protection becomes available for a fee of 1.5 per cent. It is certainly not to be regarded as a gift from the Government, although the Bill clearly indicates that funds are to be made available to the program initially from the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
There are a number of very substantial gaps in the Bill. It refers to benefits, but it does not indicate how those benefits are to be paid. I am at a complete loss as I examine the Bill. When the Minister has an opportunity, perhaps he might like to indicate to us how those benefits are to be paid. Let us assume that we are dealing with a mortgage that was renewed just at the time this plan became effective. When the new renewal comes up, the protection is paid for the full term.
By the way, a five-year mortgage is the best deal and there is no doubt about that since there is no difference in premium rates if a mortgage is taken for five years, for three years or for one year. I think the general public should be made aware of that. As a matter of fact, I think that a big blue flag should be put on all of this material to indicate to home owners that they get the best deal with a five-year term. I would have said a red flag but we are the ones who are drawing this to the attention of the public.
This Bill does not indicate that mortgagees are entitled to receive anything less than that which is provided under the terms of the mortgage. Mortgagees in fact will be paid the full amount. The home owner and CMHC will step in and jointly make the payments that must be made. I would like to know where in the Bill reference is made to who gets the money. Does the home owner receive a monthly cheque from the corporation or does the corporation pay the funds directly to the mortgagee? In any event, that is only one of the gaps in the Bill. I know we will be told that all of that will be established by regulation.
We have been waiting for this legislation for a long time. I certainly do not intend to delay it. However, I believe that it is important to examine in a forthright and honest fashion the way in which the legislation has been drafted. I do not know who the Government has retained in the Department of Justice to draft legislation, but this is, to say the very least, a dog's breakfast. As I examined the Bill, it became apparent that there was one potential for conflict after another. The word "term" is defined on page 10 of the Bill as follows:
-in relation to any borrowing of money or any loan, means a term stipulated for the repayment thereof and includes a period of extension or renewal of such a term.

May 30, 1984
National Housing Act
If one had a five-year mortgage, "term" would clearly mean that it would include a five-year renewal in the event that the mortgage referred to a potential for renewal, or it would include a renewal if that renewal were negotiated prior to the expiration of the date of the original term. However, if we examine page 11, there appears a rather interesting provision. Clause 34.82(1 )(b)(iii) states:
-the term or each of any such successive terms is not less than one year.
The question is: How can it possibly occur in the event that "term" means original term and any possible renewal thereof? It is interesting to note that "term" is defined in Clause 34.82(a) wherein it reads:
-the home owner obtains for that purpose on or after the expiry of that term;
The plan, as I understand it, contemplates obtaining by an insurance-like premium a protection for the renewal of a mortgage at a rate which is guaranteed with respect to the rate of interest in part only. Clause 34.82, which is the operative part of the Bill in terms of providing protection is, to say the very least, extremely confusing.
If that provision is confusing, I would invite Hon. Members to proceed to Clause 34.83. What I thought was the nature of the protection as explained in the immediately preceding paragraph is destroyed by providing that: "The corporation"- which is CMHC-"may, from time to time, in prescribed manner, establish rates of interest, for publication", and upon such publication the rates which are to apply to the protected loan and the base loan shall be the rates which are established by the corporation. They are to be the rates which will give rise to the extent of the protection. I say that because that is apparently what the words mean but, I cannot understand the process. If, indeed, they do provide for an abatement between the real rate paid and the rate contracted for and if they reduce that gap protection, then I would clearly ask that this matter be drawn to the attention of the public. The public is clearly of a different view.
One of the most troublesome provisions which should concern all Members of the House is the persistent reference to regulation, prescribed forms, prescribed circumstances and deemed consequences. In this 17 page Bill, regulations or prescriptions occur 55 times. What should we call a Bill which provides for such mammoth and substantial changes when, by way of regulation the heart and soul of the Bill may be removed? That is what the Bill does.
I know it is pleasant for the Government to come to the House and say, "Please pass a skeleton and we will add to it the meat. Please stick up a stake and we will stick the limbs on it." That is exactly what it is doing. We will not have to return to this troublesome place-the House of Commons-for further examination and approval or changes. If there are any mistakes, the Government will fix them by regulation.
Let us look at some of the significant provisions which may be altered by regulation. Let us look at the very heart and soul of the Bill in terms of the insuring of mortgage interest rates. As I indicated earlier, that is Clause 34.82. If we examine that Clause from the beginning it states:
(1) Subject to this Part and any regulations made under subsection 34.88(1)-
The very heart of the Bill is subject to regulations. It also makes reference to specific regulations. If we turn to Clause 34.88, among the provisions that may be changed by regulation, on page 16, under item (d) it states:
-prescribing any terms and conditions to which entering into a contract under subsection 34.82(1) shall be subject;
The place to determine the conditions which entitle people to receive their money is in the Bill itself and not in the regulations. We have already established that. People have to pay a premium of 1.5 per cent. The maximum amount of the mortgage that can be secured is $70,000. People are only entitled to recover three-quarters of the amount. It is all spelled out in the legislation. Increases of over 10 per cent interest are not entitled to reimbursement. As well, there is a 2 per cent self-insuring clause. What then does this clause mean? I do not know. Because I do not know, I should naturally be alarmed that I am called upon to pass legislation which, by the very terms of the Bill itself, authorizes the Government to step in and potentially change the main thrust of the legislation.
That is not the only place in the Bill where that kind of circumstance applies. It is sufficiently harmful that I think it requires renewed examination. Surely the Government can come before the House with a plan which is clear. It is able to spell it out in the pamphlet which has been issued. For instance, we could look at one of the provisions in the pamphlet which asks: "Can a Home owner Renew his Protection? Yes. Upon expiry of his or her original mortgage, the homeowner can extend the mortgage protection by paying an additional premium. This gives the homeowner the option of continuous protection until the mortgage is paid off."
One should examine the provisions of Bill C-37, under Clause 34.87(1) which deals with the establishment of the base loan and the protected loan-and one may be deemed to be the same as the other-and then read Clause 34.87(2), which states:
Notwithstanding subsection (1), where a home owner has been provided with protection in respect of any loan, no further protection in respect of that loan may be provided.
That is one statement in the Bill, to my mind, which is in direct contradiction with the statement which appears in the pamphlet. I believe that the Government genuinely intends that the statement which appears in the pamphlet be the law, but this provision in the Bill has, in my submission at least, the very real prospect of creating the opposite effect. If the words are intended to convey some other impression, can they not be spelled out in a fashion which Hon. Members of this House can understand? In their present form they leave me with the very distinct impression that the opposite effect from that originally intended, allegedly, by the Government, will result if this House passes this Bill in this form.
May 30, 1984

In my view, we have a responsibility-if I may deal with the way in which legislation is introduced in this place-to see that Parliament itself understands legislation it passes; not fails to understand, not delegates to someone else, not delegates to the Governor in Council. We have a parliamentary form of government, and the establishment of legislation which is the trunk of a tree on which limbs are to be hung, or which is the skeleton on which the government is to put the flesh, is not the purpose of this House. I urge the Minister, who is here, to go back to the person who is doing the drafting of Bills for him, and when this matter is referred to committee he should be prepared to make some very substantial changes which will reflect what appears to be the alleged intention of the Government.
I also believe that it is vitally important for Members of Parliament, in the event that they are to discharge their duties, to be able to understand clearly and as promptly as possible what the words mean. In addition, every time the words "prescribed" or "fixed by regulation" appear, the Minister must understand that we are denied the right to discharge the obligations placed upon us by our constituents. I find this whole method of drafting legislation to be offensive.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Are there any questions or comments? Debate.

Mr. Speaker, I take pleasure in the opportunity to contribute to this debate this afternoon on Bill C-37, which is designed to establish a mortgage interest rate protection plan. This Bill has in it a main component which is of more interest to me, that is it permits the federal Government to once again become directly involved in the delivery of a number of social housing programs which formerly had to be delivered through a number of provincial agencies.
I am happy that the Minister is in the House this afternoon. He will recall that I raised this question with him a couple of weeks ago. He told me at that time that the agreements with the provinces were short of a few minor details but they would be ironed out in due course. I am pleased in a sense to see that the ironing out which has been done resulted in eliminating the provincial jurisdiction in this area, and permitted the federal Government once again to deliver these programs directly, because that has been a more effective way, at least in my experience, in the past.
I am particularly concerned, of course, with the Rural and Native Housing Program-because of the nature of my constituency-which has been sadly neglected over the last few years. In a sense it is sad that we cannot get together in a more co-operative program of federalism which would permit the two Governments to co-operate in a more effective way. However, it seems that in all cases the federal Government insists on having its piece of plywood outside saying, "This is a federal project. Look at what we are giving you. Look at how generous we are with you. We want to remind you of that when an election comes around".
National Housing Act
Naturally, the provinces want to collect their political currencies as well when these kinds of programs are delivered and public moneys are being spent. Unfortunately, in many cases that has resulted in not delivering the programs at all because the governments cannot get together and that is, in a sense, unfortunate. I do not know what the solution is, the nature of our business being what it is. It will probably always be the case that the government which delivers these kinds of programs wants the political credit for it. As I say, I consider this unfortunate.
There are a number of positive things which I could say about this Bill, but I am very much afraid that it is my role, and the role of the Opposition, to point out the more negative features of the Bill. Let me just say from the outset that apart from the social delivery system which has now been improved upon, I do not see anything in this Bill that is worth considering. There is a lot less there than meets the eye and a lot less than was in the Throne Speech or in the announcements by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. LeBlanc) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) or, indeed, in the Bill itself.
We have a mortgage interest rate protection plan in this Bill. The Minister of Finance a few moments ago stood up in this House and told us not to worry, there is not to be any public money involved in this; that it is sort of a self-supporting, self-sustaining kind of a program; that the mortgage holders will be paying for the protection like buying life insurance or buying any other kind of insurance. What that means, in a sense, is that the mortgage holders, instead of waiting for interest rates to rise, will now have the privilege of paying their interest rates in advance.
There is a $70,000 limit on this program. That means, in many cases, if it is a five-year period, the mortgage holder will now have the privilege not only of paying the current rate of his mortgage, which is 14 per cent or 14.5 per cent, but in addition to that he may pay some interest in advance in the amount of up to $1,500. This shows how much faith the Government has in the stabilization of the market and the stabilization of interest rates.
The Minister of Finance said today during Question Period that his Government does not have a high interest rate policy. I suppose what he is saying to us is that there are no high interest rates in this country. This is just a rumour started by some ungrateful Canadians who cannot afford to renew their mortgages. The Government does not have a high interest rate policy, yet this whole Bill does nothing else but protect mortgage holders not from current high interest rates, but against future increases in interest rates. Therefore, there really is no help in there for the mortgage holder. Instead, it will create a lot of fear, anxiety and uncertainty in the marketplace because we are now saying, "Go and buy your mortgage insurance plan because the storm clouds are coming, interest rates are going to go up and we want you to protect yourself against these fluctuations".

May 30, 1984
National Housing Act
The problem is not really so much with protecting mortgage holders against high interest rates. What we on this side of the House really expected was an attack by the Government on the cause of high interest rates in the housing field. We in this country have not yet recognized that housing in a modern civilized industrial society like ours is a social right. We pretend that we have recognized that, but we really have not. Like clothing and food, housing is essential, particularly in a country like ours when it gets to 40 below. People need to have shelters, therefore it is a social right. The Government talks about this social right, but it has done very little about it. Having accepted that principle, and recognizing that the problem with the housing industry is that it fluctuates with the economy, that is to say as the economy goes up and down so do interest rates and mortgage rates, other countries have managed to separate the housing market from the rest of the money market.
I would like to give the Minister a few examples of what other countries have done to bring about effective housing policies. It is not uncommon, even today in the U.S., to have a fixed mortgage at 6 per cent. It is not at all uncommon in Britain, France and in Germany to get 40 or 50-year fixed mortgages at 5 per cent or 5.5 per cent. How is it done? What are these people doing that we are not? First of all, they recognize that housing is a social right. Secondly, they have recognized that a home owner, by virtue of being a home owner, is a productive citizen. He is a taxpayer, he buys furniture, carpets, building materials and plants for his garden. He adds to the social inventory of the country. Almost every person aspires to own a home. It is a protection against inflation and they can pass it on to their children. But what do they do? Let us look at some of the schemes in place in the United States.
We have the great problem of a shortage of capital at times. That is the reason why the National Housing Act was created. The banks and financial institutions in our country did not, for whatever reason, satisfy the need that existed. Incidentally, this country has a backlog in demand for housing, about
200,000	housing units. That is, of course, more than we are building every year. Up to April of this year, compared to last year, housing starts are down 37,000 units. That is terrible. These other countries know that housing construction is very stimulative to the economy. The lumber industry, which is in such difficulty right now, would certainly be stimulated by more effective housing programs. This applies to all sectors of the economy. Well then, what can we do? We could entice people to invest not only in their own homes but in the housing market itself.
Canadians have more money invested in term deposits in the banks than any other nation in the world. That is why it is not too wise to make comparisons between Canada and the United States. People in the U.S. tend to invest in the stock market more than do Canadians. Some 27 per cent of all adult Americans invest in the stock market, whereas in Canada it is only 7 per cent. Canadians are, I suppose, very cautious
investors. Perhaps it has to do with a little bit of ignorance about how business and the stock market work. Well, how can we get people to take their money out of the banks and put it in the housing market or small business or whatever? The way to do it in the housing market is to give them the necessary tax inducement to take money out of term deposits and put it in the housing market.
That is not new. In fact, the Government had discovered this idea, but its priorities are all wrong. You can invest money in the film industry and it is deductible from taxable income. You would not believe how much money there is available for the production of films. Well, it is very simple. The Minister would not believe how much money there would be available over night with the right inducements for people to put their money into a mortgage exchange corporation. The Minister has such an instrument. It was passed by Parliament in 1975 but it has never been declared. You pay money into a mortgage exchange corporation and the interest you earn is tax free. The interest rate, of course, is down to 6 per cent or 7 per cent. That saving would then be passed on to home builders and of course the net result would be that your earnings would be the same. If you paid tax on the interest from a 10 per cent or 11 per cent security deposit in a bank, you would be probably worse off than if you were earning 7 per cent in this other instrument. That is one way of doing it.
In 1979 we proposed the mortgage deductibility plan. You could deduct from your taxable income a portion or all of the interest that you paid on your mortgage. That resulted in a very significant saving to home owners and a very significant reduction in interest rates.
Let me tell the Minister of an even more effective and workable system. It was created about 150 years ago in Great Britain. Those governments, a co-op or a union permit people to save in advance for their homes. In Germany it is mostly the unions that manage these saving societies. It is not necessarily the potential home owner himself who does the saving. Parents and grandparents save for their children or grandchildren. Anyone who wants to save in the housing market can put money into a plan and then give it away to someone or even sell the plan for a little profit.
You put some disposable income into a mortgage exchange corporation or savings society. The money is government guaranteed. The interest rate is very low. It is 1 per cent or 2 per cent. You tailor your plan to your needs. If you need $80,000 or $100,000 10 years from now, you have a plan tailored for yourself. In 10 years you will have saved about 25, 30 or even 40 per cent of the total. You get only a very low rate of interest while you are saving. In return, when the plan matures, you get a fixed mortgage for whatever duration you wish at an interest rate which is presently, in most cases, 5.5 or 6 per cent. This happens in Great Britain, France, Italy, Austria and Germany.
These are countries which are over populated. I can fit three of these countries into my own constituency. There are 60
May 30, 1984

million people living in the Federal Republic of Germany. My nephews and nieces there all plan to build their own homes. Some of them are doing it right now. They are doing it at a fixed rate of 5.5 per cent because their fathers, and later on themselves, as they started to work, planned ahead and accepted the responsibility associated with planning your own future and building your house.
In Canada, 35 per cent of our population comes from countries which have this experience. Is it the banks that do not let you do these things because they need their pound of flesh? You are subsidizing the home owners with this nonsense. You are subsidizing the banks, the insurance corporations and the mortgage corporations. Is that the problem? Are you catering to the banks? Are you their puppet? Are you really worried about home owners? Why is it that we in Canada cannot do what other countries have done so effectively over the last 150 years? You make all kinds of comparisons with other countries all the time. These are not socialist ideas. They are effective ideas once you have accepted that housing is one of the three essential elements of life in a country like this. Why is it that you are so stubborn, so totally ignorant, and so totally devoid of any ideas? Why is it that Canadians cannot-

understanding the problem. Neither of them understand nor have ever understood the solutions.

Member know that we were unable to deliver to natives and rural people a program in British Columbia because under the law we had to have 25 per cent provincial participation and that participation, without reference to signs or credit, was not forthcoming?

May 30, 1984
National Housing Act
In fairness to the Minister, the Government was giving an undue amount of political credits. Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle). Member for Prince George-Peace River think that the Liberal Government should bring forward its policy and program on how it is going to reduce interest rates as the Liberals said they would over national television night after night during the 1980 election campaign? Member think the Liberals should explain why they allowed the interest rates to go to 21 per cent? Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in the debate, but very concerned in another way. Four years have gone by since this Government has been in power. Now we are in a situation where the Liberals are producing amendments not only to the Interest Act through Bill C-36, but also introducing amendments to the National Housing Act through Bill C-37.
This afternoon during question period we heard that we have to work together, meaning federal, provincial, and municipal governments, but when we look at Bill C-37, what do we see? We do not see federal and provincial governments working together. What we see is the federal Government going on its own. It is a sad state of affairs when we as a federal Government cannot work together with our counterparts in the provinces.
Housing to me and to the Members on this side of the House is very important. Everyone in this country should be able to have affordable housing. Everyone has a right to have a home. Let me speak about rural and native housing. There are a number of reserves in my riding of Timiskaming. Let me introduce to you, Sir, one part of my riding, the Moosonee-Moose Factory area. That area is made up of a native reserve and is in the northern part of James Bay. I went to that part of my riding last week. A housing survey was taking place. It was shocking, to say the least. In 1984 we still have people living in tents. I know that is hard to believe, but it is true. That same survey showed in addition to those living in tents two, three, and four families were living under one roof. In two or three rooms were 12, 14 and 16 individuals. I was told that in winter months, people were sleeping in the attic because that was the only warm area. Today, four years after this Government took over, we are only now debating this question. I hate to say this, but is it because there is a chance we will have an election this year and is it just an election issue? I hope not.
This year in the riding of Timiskaming we are allotted 30 homes under the Native and Rural Housing Program. That will not come close to what is required. In one area of my riding, the Moosonee-Moose Factory area, those 30 homes could be used exclusively. There are other parts to my riding,
May 30, 1984

it is a very large rural riding. There are good provisions under this program. There are needy citizens not only in Northern Ontario, but across this country. There are people living in tarpaper shacks. They have pot belly stoves. They are unable to get warm and are unable to provide for their families.
We have to go further. I strongly believe we have to do so with provincial help. We have to work together to resolve the problems in the housing industry. We cannot do it by going it alone. Once again it is determined that this Government will not work with the people. The Liberals have their own thoughts. They do not share the thoughts of Canadians. They have their way of doing things and that is the way it will be.
We intend to change that pattern in a very short period of time. Let me now come to another area. Canadians young and old have always had a dream of owning their own home. We work hard over the years to get what we hope will be affordable housing. People have pride in getting a garden, a beautiful lawn, and a home.
I want to quote something that was said on February 10, 1980, "I would want to manage the economy in such a way that interest rates would, in fact, come down because the economy would be administered in a sound way." The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that in an interview with a reporter from The Toronto Star. Since that date I have friends, and I have colleagues who have friends, who have lost their homes because of this Government's policies and the increasing mortgage rates.
The mortgage interest rate policy of the Government has not been good for Canadians. The mortgage rate in 1974 was 11.88 per cent, in 1981 it was 21.46 per cent, and in 1984 it was 14.25 per cent. Approximately 2.2 jobs are created with every home built in the country. Coming from a resource-based area, I know that means employment not only directly in the construction industry but in the steel, forest and other related industries in the riding of Timiskaming and throughout northern Ontario. The adjustable seasonal rate is 166,000 or
22.5	per cent unemployed people in the construction industry across the country. It is a shameful number and it is due to the high interest rate policy of the present Government.
If a mortgage with a base rate of 12 per cent is renewed at 17 per cent, the first two percentage points are not covered by the insurance. speechtext: Are there any further questions? The Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hov-debo) on debate.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate on Bill C-37, which is

May 30, 1984
National Housing Act
supposedly to provide insurance against rising mortgage interest rates. However, it should be called a Bill to insure against government incompetence, because that is what it really attempts to do. It attempts to patch up the mistakes of the Government of a few years ago, mistakes which have caused the situation where people are losing their homes because of high interest rates and fluctuating interest rates. Instead of suggesting, as this Bill does, putting in place an insurance plan against high mortgage interest rates, it should be possible to put in place a set rate mortgage such as we had for many years.
It was brought in by Diefenbaker in 1959.

That could possibly be so. I would not want to question the Hon. Member on that. A fixed affordable interest rate on long-term mortgages for many years did for the housing industry what was necessary. It did not hamper the building of houses. However, that fixed interest rate was removed by the then Minister of Public Works, Mr. Hellyer, to open up the market so that builders would become involved in constructing affordable houses and would be able to sell them somewhat easier. The record will show that as a result of opening up the market and fluctuating interest rates, for a number of years housing starts declined and that the building industry was not helped. In fact, it made it somewhat more difficult for people to obtain affordable housing and, consequently, somewhat more difficult for people even to find housing.
Bill C-37 allows for interest rates to increase approximately 3 per cent or 3.5 per cent without any assistance being provided. That is a 25 per cent increase on interest rates with respect to the level of present interest rates. I do not consider these to be essentially affordable interest rates.
Instead of attempting to establish an insurance policy to protect against increasing interest rates, I suggest that the Government should withdraw the Bill and introduce measures to assure long-term, fixed and affordable interest rates that would encourage people to buy homes.
For example, I lived in New Zealand for a number of years. That country was in the process of trying to increase the amount of available housing. Therefore, that government only charged 1.5 per cent interest as a service charge to those who wanted to build or buy a home. These funds kept revolving so that when someone paid off their home, the funds were made available to someone else. This process went on for many years and the money was used repeatedly to help people build homes. In approximately 15 years, the amount of available housing increased by 20 per cent. That is the sort of approach that the Government should take.
Once the requirement for homes is established and people are able to buy them, the economy is affected in many ways. When a home is constructed, it is not only those in the construction industry who are involved but those who work in the factories that manufacture furniture, appliances and other
fixtures for the home. This contributes to the economy which, in turn, improves the situation in the country and allows more people to buy homes.
It is only logical to create an economy that easily and quickly satisfies the needs of the people. Instead, the Government's policies have been designed to meet the needs for profit by the banks and other financial institutions. They do not meet the needs of the people who need shelter or those who pay up to 40 per cent of their income for that shelter. This Bill will not solve any of the problems of those who require housing. It does not even solve the problems of those who may be able to buy a home. Those who are paying $250 a month rent and want to buy a home might not do so if they believe that interest rates will increase by 3.5 per cent in the near future. This is true even if they have a reasonable initial interest rate. Of course, that is not possible right now.
What is the basic purpose of this Bill? While it is supposed to enhance the possibility of owning a home, it does everything but that. If an individual who earns $1,000 or $1,500 a month is paying $500 a month for a home, receiving assistance only after interest rates increase by 3.5 per cent is not enough to be encouraged to buy a home. Furthermore, since interest rates are already high, any increase in interest rates may eliminate the possibility of buying a home. Even a 3.5 per cent increase may not be affordable to some home owners. There are many people who earn $1,200 or $1,500 a month and are paying $600 on their mortgage. They cannot afford an increase of $50, and 3.5 per cent is much more than they can afford. In fact, I suspect there are many people who cannot even afford an increase of 1.5 per cent which is required for them to take advantage of this insurance plan.
One of the purposes of this Bill is to guarantee against increases in interest rates. This Bill does not do so because it provides for a basic 3.5 per cent increase before the plan takes effect. Our old laws used to allow a mortgage to be paid off after five years, with a three-month penalty period. This possibility is removed as a result of this Bill. Home owners who have owned their homes for more than five years will not have the possibility to save enough money to pay off their mortgage without a large penalty.
On many occasions in the House, Members from the NDP and the Official Opposition have told the Minister responsible for housing and the Minister of Finance (Mr. La.'onde) about people who are trying to pay off mortgages that have gone out of sight as a result of high interest rates. When they have attempted to do so, they have been charged up to $8,000 in penalties, notwithstanding the three-month interest rate penalty. We have raised questions about those situations that have made it impossible for people to pay off their mortgages and avoid the 19 per cent and 20 per cent interest rates which some people faced. In fact, there are still some people in my constituency who are attempting to get rid of 19 per cent mortgages.
Rather than increase security for some people, this Bill removes some of the security of those who had an opportunity to get out of large mortgage payments from the past. This Bill
May 30, 1984

is likely to decrease the amount of affordable housing for Canadians. It is estimated that we currently need approximately one million homes in Canada. If the Government were to establish a logical interest rate structure, without worrying about how much the banks and other financial institutions will make, it could instruct the banks to allot 10 per cent of loans for housing mortgages and they will receive 7 per cent of that. This was done for a number of years. We did that for a good number of years. If we did it again, the number of houses that would be built would be increased very quickly because people would begin to build their own homes or pay the construction industry to build their homes for them.
It is very sad that the financial structure of the country has become more important to this Government than the need for good, affordable housing. It is sad that banks and mortgage companies are more important to the Government than the need for good, affordable housing. Housing is a necessity. I am not even sure that banks are necessary.
When the Social Credit Party first came to power in Alberta, it was probably the first group of socially-minded people to tangle with the banks of Canada. At that time, members of that Government tried to put in place a system which would make use of the productivity and resources of Alberta and its people. They said that they did not need the banks and did not have to give 10 per cent or 20 per cent of their productivity away. They felt they could circulate the money with their own province and establish a financial structure which would be of benefit to Albertans rather than to large banks and financial corporations. The Aberhart Government passed what it thought was the required legislation which was then struck down by the Supreme Court of Canada. The Supreme Court would not allow the Aberhart Government to put in place a structure which would allow Albertans to use their own resources and their own productivity in the way they wanted.
Almost the same kind of thing is happening now. People who want to build a house and live in it cannot do so because the Government feels that we must not interfere with the ability of a bank to make money. There are many people in this country who are quite willing to begin to build houses and, with a little bit of help from the Government, they would do so. I am speaking of course of the large number of people who would like to start co-operative housing projects.
As well, there are a number of people in the country who are making war on that possibility. Builders' associations and other financially-based institutions have very strong lobbies that come to see Members of Parliament here in Ottawa to tell us that co-op housing should not be subsidized by the Government. Unfortunately, the Government is listening to that lobby and not to the millions who want affordable housing. The Government is listening to the banks and the mortgage companies, the companies that will make money on the buying and selling of houses. Consequently, the Government is not ready to allow co-operative housing projects to go ahead.
National Housing Act
Co-operative housing has proven its effectiveness by supplying the community-based and socially integrated housing that is necessary for the people who find it difficult to get together enough money to build a house. It has proved effective for those who do not want to spend $80,000 on a house just to spend another $160,000 on interest in the next 15 years. Rather, they would like to make a commitment to pay for that house. Under the circumstances which have been put in place by the Government and which the Government is keeping in place, those people will pay $80,000 for a house and over the next 15 years will pay another $160,000. They will pay for that house three times. The builder of the house will only receive $80,000 but the person who has bought the house will pay for it three times. The Government is going along with that idea.
Housing is a necessity and a right, and it is something that we in this Parliament should stand up for as best we can and for as long as we can. Instead, we are discussing a Bill that does none of the things that are needed to increase available housing. It does none of the things that are needed to make it possible for those with lower incomes to buy houses. A few years ago, the Government, the Official Opposition and our Party made a commitment to the people of Canada that we would make affordable housing a major part of our platform and we have ceased to do so.
